title: How To Find God In A Five Cent Fruit
author: Sam Alaimo
source: Stoic Wisdoms (stoicwisdoms.com), guest post from What then?, September 17, 2026
summary: In a guest essay for Stoic Wisdoms, former Navy SEAL and writer Sam Alaimo diagnoses a 'civilizational malady': having removed the burden of nature, modern people carry the heavier burden of freedom from it, expressed as a chronic craving for the next vacation, promotion or imagined future, and a willful blindness to what is already present. He grounds the argument in a household practice of writing one or two sentences a day about something small, and in a vivid comparison of Cotton Candy and Moon Drop grapes. The essay's pivot is a passage from Epictetus rebuking a student who longs to see Athens and the Acropolis while ignoring the sun, moon, stars and sea in front of him. Alaimo reads this as a confession that the desire to be elsewhere is a refusal to be content with oneself, and frames the choice as slavery to relative comparison versus a creed of absolute awe. He is careful to say this is not a call to low standards but a paradox of character: the only way to be satisfied with an extraordinary future is to be extraordinarily satisfied with the everyday. Classified as Leadership for its focus on personal character and self-mastery, consistent with prior Stoic Wisdoms entries.
points: Alaimo names a two-part malady: a chronic desire for the next moment, sustained by blindness to the fact that what we seek over there already exists here.
His practical antidote is a kitchen Household Diary of one or two sentences a day, which forces attention onto a single ordinary object or moment.
Epictetus' rebuke of the student who longs for Athens is read as a diagnosis that wanting to be elsewhere is a confession of not being content to be oneself.
The essay frames the basic choice as slavery to relative comparisons versus freedom through absolute awe, where each achieved future simply becomes the next stepping stone.
He insists this is not an argument for low standards but a paradox: satisfaction with an extraordinary future depends on being extraordinarily satisfied with the everyday.
quotes: Civilization is strange. We removed the burden of nature only to find a far greater burden—the burden of freedom from nature.

First, a chronic desire for the next moment: the next vacation, promotion, phone, or blissful image in our skull of a perfect future, and all we need to do to earn it is be miserable just a little while longer… or so we tell ourselves. And second, to keep this desire active, the malady demands a willful blindness to a cosmic truth—what we are seeking over there already exists right here.
The act of stopping and putting ink to paper cuts everything else away but the singular object of our focus for the briefest of moments.
And yet… the astronomical difference between these two types of grapes is as nothing compared to the difference between the grapes and everything else we could be thinking about as we eat them.
What is Epictetus telling us? That our desire to be somewhere else is in fact a confession we are not content to be ourselves.
It seems we are born with a simple choice: we may make of ourselves slaves to relative comparisons, or we can choose to be free men and women in obedience to the creed of absolute awe.

We crave to bring our vision of the future to reality, and yet once we get it, suddenly it is worthless, and it becomes a mere stepping stone to a better vision of the future. It is a bitter irony that it is a vision we may never even live to see.

This is not a call to abandon the future and live a life of low standards. Far from it. Rather, it is to learn to love a paradox: the only way to be satisfied with an extraordinary future, which will itself become the everyday, is to be extraordinarily satisfied with the everyday.
